---
title: "Notes on parameters interpretation and priors"
format: html
---

In the context of the hierarchical multi-site model, the selection of priors and the interpretation of parameters like $\beta$ are foundational to the demographic inference.

## Interpretation of $\beta$ (Entry Probability)
In this state-space framework, $\beta$ represents the entry probability. Biologically, this parameter quantifies recruitment into the study population. It is defined as the probability that an individual enters the observable population at occasion $k$, provided it was not already present at occasion $k-1$. In an open population model, this recruitment is an aggregate measure encompassing both births (natality) and immigration into the study area. By allowing $\beta$ to vary by area and session (array[N_areas, K]), the model accounts for spatial and temporal heterogeneity in how new individuals join the population.

## Selection of Weakly Informative Priors
The model utilizes weakly informative priors to strike a balance between biological realism and data-driven estimation. These priors are designed to prevent the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampler from exploring nonsensical parameter space while ensuring the data remains the primary driver of the posterior distribution.

Inclusion ($\psi$) and Entry ($\beta$): These parameters are assigned a $\text{Beta}(1, 1)$ prior. This is mathematically equivalent to a $\text{Uniform}(0, 1)$ distribution, representing a non-informative state where all probabilities are initially considered equally likely.

Global Mortality ($\mu$): The prior $\mu \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1)$ with a lower=0 constraint results in a half-normal distribution. This favors lower mortality rates (high survival) but possesses sufficient variance to accommodate higher mortality if the capture data indicates rapid individual turnover.

Detection Intercepts ($\alpha_p$): A $\text{Normal}(0, 2)$ prior is applied on the logit scale. This is weakly informative because it covers a vast range of detection probabilities once back-transformed (approximately $2\%$ to $98\%$), effectively allowing the model to adapt to various sampling conditions across the study sites.

## Addressing Potential Pitfalls
While the hierarchical structure is advantageous for "borrowing strength" across sites, it introduces the shrinkage effect. Because all areas share a single global mortality rate ($\mu$), the estimates for individual sites are "pulled" toward the global average. This is a deliberate trade-off: it reduces the variance of estimates in data-poor areas (like S1870 or R1200) at the potential cost of a slight bias if a specific site's true mortality deviates significantly from the mean. Furthermore, for the most sparse sites, the model's ability to distinguish between true low abundance and low detection relies heavily on this hierarchical information sharing.
